Babylon. This Mesopotamian city-state rose to imperial dominance twice. First under Hammurabi, who lived from 1792 to 1750 BCE, conquering and unifying southern Mesopotamia and codifying the famous Code of Hammurabi. And again under Nebuchadnezzar II, who ruled from 605 to 562 BCE, expanding the empire to its territorial peak and rebuilding the city as a magnificent administrative and cultural center.

Hammurabi inherited a small city-state and conquered a regional empire in southern Mesopotamia through military campaigns and diplomacy. The Code of Hammurabi—a formal legal text of 282 laws—established the principle that rulers enforce uniform law. It established social hierarchy and punishment proportional to crime, the famous "eye for an eye" principle. Under Hammurabi, Babylon became a center of mathematics and astronomy. Scribes developed algebraic notation and predicted lunar cycles centuries before Greek astronomy.

The Neo-Babylonian period began with Nebuchadnezzar II, who conquered Syria and Phoenicia and besieged Jerusalem in 586 BCE, deporting the Hebrew elite and establishing Babylonian hegemony over the Levant. Nebuchadnezzar rebuilt Babylon into a showpiece. The Ishtar Gate, the Tower of Babel, and the Hanging Gardens, possibly, made it the ancient world's most magnificent city. The empire maintained power through a bureaucratic system of provinces, standing armies, and administrative schools, inheriting the Akkadian model and perfecting it.

Babylon fell to the Persian Cyrus the Great in 539 BCE without a siege. The populace welcomed the Persians as liberators from the authoritarian last Babylonian kings. Babylon remained a major city under Persian, Seleucid, and Parthian rule but never regained empire status.

Babylon represents the maturation of Mesopotamian imperial culture. Where Akkad pioneered centralized rule through military force, Babylon added law as a legitimizing tool. A monarch was now accountable to public codes, not just military success. The Code of Hammurabi ensured that conquest had a civilian face—subjects expected justice, not just obedience. The Neo-Babylonian period showed the apotheosis of this model: magnificent architecture, advanced science, and cultural prestige made Babylon aspirational, not merely feared.
